name: Exemestane
lead: Exemestane, sold under the brand name Aromasin, is an oral steroidal aromatase inhibitor: it permanently inactivates the enzyme that converts androgens into oestrogens. In medicine it is used for hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer in postmenopausal women, and the US label lists adjuvant treatment after two to three years of tamoxifen and treatment of advanced disease that has progressed on tamoxifen.[1][23] It is a prescription medicine.

Its appearance relevance comes from oestrogen's role in the body. Oestrogen helps drive the closing of the growth plates in adolescents, and lowering it is the reason aromatase inhibitors are discussed for height, and, in adult men, for managing oestrogen-related effects such as gynecomastia and water retention during hormone or anabolic use.[23][24] On looksmax.org, teenagers describe taking it to keep growth plates open, often alongside growth hormone, and compare it with anastrozole and letrozole; some call it the gentler or more androgenic choice, while others report hair or hormonal problems.[2][3][4][5][6][7][8]

Published human research on exemestane is overwhelmingly in breast cancer, from the Intergroup Exemestane Study to the SOFT and TEXT trials in premenopausal women.[10][11][13][14][15] Wikipedia's broader article on aromatase inhibitors describes their use in boys for growth as experimental, and cites a study in which letrozole increased near-final height in boys with constitutional delay of puberty.[24] No trial of exemestane for height in healthy adolescents was found. Label warnings include reductions in bone mineral density and fetal harm.[1]

paras: The US label indicates exemestane for adjuvant treatment of postmenopausal women with oestrogen-receptor-positive early breast cancer who have had two to three years of tamoxifen, and for advanced breast cancer progressing after tamoxifen.[1] The Intergroup Exemestane Study and an earlier randomised trial examined switching from tamoxifen to exemestane,[10][11] and Wikipedia reports that two to three years of exemestane after tamoxifen was generally more effective than five years of tamoxifen alone.[23] Grokipedia reports a 24% relative reduction in recurrence or death in the former.[12]

In premenopausal women, exemestane with ovarian suppression was compared with tamoxifen in the SOFT and TEXT trials, with long-term follow-up reported in 2023.[13][14][15][27] A 2011 trial of exemestane for breast-cancer prevention in 4,560 postmenopausal women at increased risk reported a 65% reduction in invasive breast cancer versus placebo.[16][23] In advanced HR-positive, HER2-negative disease it is combined with everolimus, an mTOR inhibitor, in the BOLERO-2 trial.[17][25] Guidelines from the American Society of Clinical Oncology cover its place among endocrine therapies for metastatic disease.[26]

Interest centres on height and on oestrogen control. Posters ask how to keep growth plates open until growth hormone can be obtained, or whether exemestane alone is worthwhile at 15; replies note that growth plates commonly close between 15 and 21 depending on puberty timing.[2][3] A comparison thread has a user stating that exemestane increases androgens, which they consider beneficial, and another recommending a non-steroidal inhibitor.[5] Thread titles claim that exemestane is androgenic and discuss voice pitch, oestrogen and body fat.[18][19]

Among adult men, aromatase inhibitors are used off-label to control oestrogen during testosterone therapy or anabolic steroid use, with the aim of limiting gynecomastia and fluid retention, and exemestane appears in post-cycle regimens; Wikipedia notes that clinical evidence for this is limited.[23][24][12] Grokipedia cites a cross-sectional study of 50 male anabolic-steroid users in which exemestane was the most commonly used aromatase inhibitor.[12]

Aromatase converts androgens to oestrogens; in postmenopausal women peripheral conversion is the main source of circulating oestrogen. Exemestane is a steroidal, type I inhibitor that acts as a false substrate and binds irreversibly, in contrast with the non-steroidal triazoles anastrozole and letrozole, which compete reversibly with the substrate.[1][23][24] Its structure is related to androstenedione, and a crystal-structure paper describes a related compound.[20][23]

Wikipedia reports an oral bioavailability of about 60%, about 90% plasma protein binding, maximal aromatase inhibition after two to three days, and metabolism by CYP3A4 and aldo-keto reductases; roughly equal amounts are excreted in urine and faeces.[23] Grokipedia gives a different bioavailability figure and reports 85-95% oestrogen suppression in postmenopausal women.[12] In a study of young men cited by Wikipedia, oestrogen suppression ranged from about 35% for oestradiol to about 70% for oestrone.[23]

Forum claims that exemestane is androgenic trace to a metabolite, 17-hydroexemestane, which Grokipedia says binds the androgen receptor much more strongly than the parent drug, although the same page also describes it elsewhere as inactive.[12] Wikipedia says androgenic effects such as acne and weight gain are mostly linked to doses well above therapeutic ones.[23] Controlled data on this in healthy young people were not found.

The label reports hot flushes (21% versus 20% with tamoxifen), fatigue (16%), arthralgia (15%), headache, insomnia and increased sweating as the most common reactions in early breast cancer, with reductions in bone mineral density seen over time and a recommendation to assess vitamin D beforehand. It states that exemestane can cause fetal harm.[1] Wikipedia adds lymphocyte decreases in about 20% of patients and notes that single doses up to 800 mg were tolerated in overdose reports.[23] A 2025 JAMA Ophthalmology article describes exemestane-associated bilateral maculopathy.[9]

Wikipedia's aromatase inhibitor article says bone and joint effects are established in women and that men do not appear to show the same bone effects, while listing slowed bone maturation among adverse events in the young.[24] Rifampicin lowers exemestane exposure by about half, and oestrogens are expected to reduce its effect.[23]

Forum threads include a report titled as exemestane having nuked someone's hair, and one titled as nuking oestrogen permanently; these are anecdotes.[7][8] One thread title discusses whether exemestane affects IGF-1.[29]

Human trials are in breast cancer: the Intergroup Exemestane Study,[11] the 2004 randomised trial of exemestane after tamoxifen,[10] SOFT/TEXT in premenopausal women,[13][14][15][27] prevention in postmenopausal women,[16] and combination studies with everolimus.[17][25] Registered trials include exemestane in endometrial and prostate cancer.[21][22]

No studies of exemestane for height or other cosmetic aims in healthy people were found. Related research on other aromatase inhibitors in boys is described on Wikipedia, which cites a letrozole study reporting increased near-final height in boys with constitutional delay of puberty, and calls the approach experimental.[24]

Grokipedia reports that exemestane was discovered by Pharmacia in Italy, with a synthesis patented by Farmitalia Carlo Erba in the late 1980s and preclinical development from 1986; Wikipedia lists the code name FCE-24304 and files it under drugs developed by Pfizer.[12][23] Europe approved it for advanced breast cancer in December 1998 and the FDA on 21 October 1999, with the US adjuvant indication following in October 2005; generics reached the EU in 2010 and the US in 2011.[12][23] It is one of the second-generation steroidal inhibitors that followed formestane, the first aromatase inhibitor tested in humans in 1982, from the work of Angela Brodie.[24]

Exemestane is prescription-only in the US and UK.[23] It is on the World Anti-Doping Agency prohibited list among aromatase inhibitors; Wikipedia says it is used in doping to raise LH and FSH and to counter gynecomastia and water retention.[23] Grokipedia says it has been prohibited since 2001 for male athletes and reports athlete suspensions.[12]

Threads cover protocols and use with growth hormone, and many are started by minors.[2][3][28] A poster who wanted to keep growth plates open says they took it after a doctor declined growth-plate surgery.[2] A reply in one thread states that non-steroidal inhibitors always win because the androgenic side effects of steroidal ones are mild.[5] Some users cast it as part of a pharmaceutical stack alongside other hormone drugs.[19]

timeline.event: Formestane, the first aromatase inhibitor tested in humans, enters clinical trials.[24]
Pharmacia begins preclinical development of exemestane, per Grokipedia.[12]

The World Anti-Doping Agency prohibits it for male athletes, per Grokipedia.[12]

US indication expanded to adjuvant switching, per Grokipedia.[12]

SOFT/TEXT results of exemestane with ovarian suppression published.[14]

lore.intro: Exemestane is discussed on looksmax.org mainly by teenagers weighing it against anastrozole and letrozole for height, with side threads on androgenic effects and hair.[2][5][18]

claims.claim: Exemestane keeps growth plates open and adds height
claims.believers: Teenage posters use it alone or with growth hormone for this reason and discuss protocols.[2][3][28]
claims.experts: No trial in healthy adolescents was found; Wikipedia describes aromatase-inhibitor use for growth in boys as experimental, and the label warns of bone mineral density loss.[24][1]

claims.claim: Exemestane is androgenic and therefore beneficial
claims.believers: Posters cite its androgenic metabolite and argue this offsets oestrogen loss.[5][18]
claims.experts: Grokipedia reports a metabolite with high androgen-receptor affinity, while Wikipedia ties androgenic effects to high doses; no controlled data exist in healthy people.[12][23]

claims.claim: Steroidal inhibitors are milder than non-steroidal ones
claims.believers: Some users call exemestane the gentler option; others say non-steroidal drugs always win.[5][6]
claims.experts: The two classes differ in mechanism, irreversible versus reversible binding; no head-to-head data in this population were found.[23][24]

claims.claim: Exemestane can permanently suppress oestrogen or cause hair loss
claims.believers: Users report such outcomes in thread titles.[7][8]
claims.experts: The label lists bone loss and other adverse reactions; permanence of suppression is not addressed.[1]

claims.claim: Aromatase inhibitors control gynecomastia in men on hormones
claims.believers: Adult users take them in post-cycle regimens to hold oestrogen down.[12]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes off-label use during testosterone therapy; Grokipedia calls clinical evidence limited and inconsistent.[24][12]

card.summary: A steroidal breast-cancer aromatase inhibitor teen heightmaxxers favour as the 'milder' option; no trials in healthy adolescents.
card.note: Label warns of bone density loss and fetal harm; height use is off-label and untested.

quick.overview:
Exemestane (Aromasin) is a prescription aromatase inhibitor for postmenopausal breast cancer. On looksmax.org, mostly teenagers discuss it for keeping growth plates open and adding height, often with growth hormone.

No trial has tested this in healthy adolescents. Users debate it against anastrozole and letrozole.
quick.mechanism: It irreversibly inactivates aromatase, reducing oestrogen production, and is a steroid structurally related to androstenedione. Lower oestrogen is thought to delay growth-plate fusion.
quick.risks: The label lists bone density loss, hot flushes, fatigue, joint pain and fetal harm; a maculopathy report exists. Forum users report hair and hormone problems. Prescription-only; height use is off-label.

chain: Oral aromatase inhibitor lowers oestrogen production
Lower oestrogen slows growth-plate fusion in adolescents
Longer growth window, discussed as a way to gain height alongside growth hormone
angle.text: Heightmaxxers use exemestane in the hope that less oestrogen keeps growth plates open longer, and adult men on hormone regimens use aromatase inhibitors to hold oestrogen down and limit gynecomastia and water retention. The growth idea is a community theory rooted in how oestrogen drives growth-plate closure.
